\chapter{Verbs of the Mind}
\label{ch:pt-mind-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I think, understand, read and write in Portuguese, produce the broken row ler shares with ver, and name the English words each of the four verbs left behind.}

The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after escrever the reader produces all four first-person forms in one run - penso, entendo, leio, escrevo - names escrito as the Latin scriptum, and re-derives the propped-up e- that turned scribere into escrever and stare into estar.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pensar]{pensar — thinking, and the scales it came from}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-pensar}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter gave you the nine verbs Portuguese cannot do without. This one adds four that all happen inside your head — and the first of them weighs things.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: A plain -ar verb, and the small word after it}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{penso} & nós \textbf{pensamos} \\
tu \textbf{pensas} & vocês/eles \textbf{pensam} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{pensa} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No surprises in the endings: \emph{pensar} runs exactly like \emph{falar}, the first verb you met. What has to be learned is the word that follows it. Portuguese thinks \textbf{in} a thing, not about it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Penso em ti.} — \textquotedblleft{}I think of you.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Penso que sim.} — \textquotedblleft{}I think so.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Pensar em} for whatever you have in mind; \emph{pensar que} for an opinion. In everyday Brazilian speech the opinion verb is more often \textbf{achar} — \emph{acho que sim} — a verb whose plain meaning is \textquotedblleft{}to find.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pensar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{pēnsāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to weigh out carefully,\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{pendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hang\textquotedblright{} — because a Roman weighed a thing by \textbf{hanging} it from a balance. To think, on that picture, is to put two things on the scales.

English owns the whole family. From the weighing half: \textbf{pensive}, and \textbf{ponder}, which is \emph{ponderāre} from \emph{pondus}, a weight. From the paying half — coins were weighed out before they were counted — \textbf{pension}, \textbf{compensate}, \textbf{dispense}, \textbf{expense} and \textbf{expend}, \textbf{stipend}, \textbf{recompense}. And from the hanging half: \textbf{pendulum}, \textbf{pendant}, \textbf{pending}, \textbf{depend} (\textquotedblleft{}to hang from\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{suspend}, \textbf{append}, \textbf{impending}. Spanish, another daughter of Latin, put the same verb on its coin: a \emph{\textbf{peso}} is a weight.

\textbf{achar} has its own history — Latin \emph{afflāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to breathe upon,\textquotedblright{} a hunter's word for catching a scent on the air. So the everyday Brazilian \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{} is really \textquotedblleft{}I find.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}penso, pensas, pensa, pensamos, pensam\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Penso em ti\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Penso que sim\textquotedblright{}
  \item knowing beside thinking — \textquotedblleft{}sei\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}penso\textquotedblright{}
  \item the weighing family — \textquotedblleft{}pensive · ponder · pension · pendulum\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{pensar}. (\textbf{Penso, pensas, pensa, pensamos, pensam}.) Which small word follows it when someone is on your mind? (\emph{\textbf{Em}} — \emph{penso em ti}.) What did \emph{pēnsāre} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{weigh out}\textquotedblright{}.) So what is a \emph{pendulum} doing? (\textbf{Hanging} — from \emph{pendere}.) And which verb from the last chapter says \textquotedblleft{}I know a fact\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Sei}}.) Next: understanding.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entender / compreender]{entender / compreender — reaching for it, or grabbing all of it}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-entender-compreender}



\begin{quote}
Weighing a thought was the last lesson. This one is the moment the thought lands — and Portuguese has two verbs for it, built on two pictures.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The everyday one, and the fuller one}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{entender — every day} & \textbf{compreender — a shade deeper} \\
\midrule
\textbf{entendo, entendes, entende, entendemos, entendem} & \textbf{compreendo, compreendes, compreende, compreendem} \\
Não entendo. — I don't understand. & Compreendo a situação. — I grasp the situation. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are ordinary \emph{-er} verbs, and in most sentences either one is correct. \textbf{Entender} is the workhorse: \emph{Não entendo}, \emph{Entendeu?}, \emph{Entendes?} \textbf{Compreender} carries more weight — understanding a thing through, or taking someone's side of it — and it does a second job English gives to another word entirely: \emph{o preço compreende tudo}, \textquotedblleft{}the price \textbf{includes} everything.\textquotedblright{}

If only one sticks, make it \emph{entender}. \textbf{Não entendo} may be the single most useful sentence a beginner owns.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{entender} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{intendere}}: \emph{in-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{tendere} (\textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}). To understand was to \textbf{stretch your attention toward} a thing. English keeps the family whole: \textbf{intend} and \textbf{intention} — the same verb, meaning barely moved — plus \textbf{intense}, \textbf{tend}, \textbf{tendency}, \textbf{tension}, \textbf{extend}, \textbf{pretend} (\textquotedblleft{}to stretch in front\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{contend}, \textbf{attend}, \textbf{portend}. And the things that literally stretch: a \textbf{tent}, a \textbf{tendon}.

\textbf{compreender} $\leftarrow$ \emph{\textbf{comprehendere}}: \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{prehendere} (\textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{}). Not reaching this time but \textbf{grabbing}, and grabbing all of it at once — \textbf{comprehend}, \textbf{comprehensive}, \textbf{apprehend}, \textbf{prehensile}. Worn down through French, that same \emph{prehendere} also gives \textbf{prison} (a \textquotedblleft{}seizing\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{prize}, \textbf{enterprise}, and \textbf{surprise}, which is \emph{super-prehendere}, \textquotedblleft{}seized from above.\textquotedblright{}

Flag the false friend: English \textbf{understand} belongs to neither family. It is Germanic, and its own picture is standing close among things.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}entendo, entendes, entende, entendemos, entendem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Não entendo\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Compreendo a situação\textquotedblright{}
  \item thinking, then understanding — \textquotedblleft{}penso\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}entendo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the stretching family — \textquotedblleft{}intend · intense · extend · tendon\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I don't understand.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Não entendo}}.) Which of the two also means \textquotedblleft{}to include\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Compreender}}.) What does \emph{tendere} mean, and what is \emph{in-tendere} doing? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{stretch}\textquotedblright{}; stretching \textbf{toward} a thing.) Taken apart, what is a \emph{surprise}? (\emph{Super-prehendere} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seized from above}\textquotedblright{}.) Is English \emph{understand} a relative? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic.) And \emph{pensar}'s root meaning? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{weigh}\textquotedblright{}.) Next: reading.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ler]{ler — a verb that gathers, worn down to three letters}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-ler}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ver}, \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} was three letters and irregular. \textbf{Ler}, \textquotedblleft{}to read,\textquotedblright{} is three letters and irregular in exactly the same way — and for the same reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: leio, lê, leem}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{leio} & nós \textbf{lemos} \\
tu \textbf{lês} & vocês/eles \textbf{leem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{lê} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say them slowly. \textbf{Leio} has grown a \emph{y}-glide in the middle. \textbf{Lê} is a single vowel held up by a circumflex. \textbf{Leem} is two \emph{e}'s in a row, and Portuguese pronounces both of them. \textbf{Não leio muito} — \textquotedblleft{}I don't read much.\textquotedblright{}

This is not random damage. It is the very row \emph{ver} uses — \emph{vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem} — and the one \emph{crer}, \textquotedblleft{}to believe,\textquotedblright{} uses too: \emph{creio, crês, crê, cremos, creem}. Learn the row once and three verbs come with it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ler} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{legere}}, whose first meaning was not reading at all. It was \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to gather, to pick, to choose}.\textquotedblright{} Reading was the metaphor — gathering letters up with the eye — and the metaphor won.

The shrinking is regular, and you have already met it. Latin \emph{legere} lost its \emph{-g-} between vowels, exactly as \emph{manus} lost its \emph{-n-} to give \emph{mão}; that leaves \emph{leer}, whose two vowels then collapse into one. \textbf{Ler} is what is left, and the circumflex on \emph{lê} is the record of the collapse.

English took both halves of \emph{legere}. The gathering half: \textbf{collect}, \textbf{select}, \textbf{elect} (\textquotedblleft{}to pick out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{intellect} (\textquotedblleft{}to choose between\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{diligent}, \textbf{neglect} (\textquotedblleft{}not to gather up\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{elegant}, which first meant choosy. The reading half: \textbf{legible}, \textbf{lecture}, \textbf{lectern}, \textbf{legend} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be read\textquotedblright{}), and — through French \emph{leçon} — the word \textbf{lesson} itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}leio, lês, lê, lemos, leem\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same row for seeing — \textquotedblleft{}vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Não leio muito\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Não entendo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the gathering family — \textquotedblleft{}collect · select · elect · legend\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{ler}, then the same row for \emph{ver}. (\textbf{Leio, lês, lê, lemos, leem}; \textbf{vejo, vês, vê, vemos, veem}.) What did \emph{legere} mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{}, and what went missing on the way to \emph{ler}? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{gather}, to pick, to choose\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{\textbf{-g-}}, between vowels, as in \emph{mão} from \emph{manus}.) Where is that root in English? (\textbf{Legible}, \textbf{lecture}, \textbf{legend}, \textbf{lesson}.) Next: writing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[escrever]{escrever — scratching, and the e- that props up an s}

\label{lesson:PT-C19-escrever}



\begin{quote}
Reading came last; writing is its partner. And this verb carries a spelling rule that will unlock dozens of other Portuguese words for you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The forms, and a participle you already own}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{escrevo} & nós \textbf{escrevemos} \\
tu \textbf{escreves} & vocês/eles \textbf{escrevem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{escreve} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A plain \emph{-er} verb, endings identical to \emph{entender}. The irregularity sits elsewhere: the past participle is \textbf{escrito}, never \emph{escrevido}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Já escrevi a carta.} — \textquotedblleft{}I already wrote the letter.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Está escrito.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is written.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Escrito} is the Latin \emph{scriptum} barely touched — which means \textbf{escrito} and English \textbf{script} are one word arriving twice.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{escrever} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{scrībere}}, \textquotedblleft{}to scratch, to incise,\textquotedblright{} because writing began as cutting marks into wax, clay, or bark. Its participle stem \emph{script-} is among the most productive things English ever borrowed: \textbf{scribe}, \textbf{scribble}, \textbf{script}, \textbf{scripture}, \textbf{describe} and \textbf{description}, \textbf{prescribe}, \textbf{subscribe}, \textbf{transcribe}, \textbf{inscribe}, \textbf{ascribe}, \textbf{conscript}, \textbf{circumscribe}, \textbf{postscript} — and \textbf{manuscript}, which is \emph{manus} plus \emph{scriptum}, \textquotedblleft{}written by the hand.\textquotedblright{} Old English borrowed the verb early and wore it down to \textbf{shrive} and \textbf{shrift}, the confession words behind \emph{Shrove Tuesday}.

Now the rule. Latin \emph{scrībere} opens with \emph{sc-}, and Iberian mouths would not start a word that way, so they propped a vowel in front of it. It happened without exception:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{scrībere} $\to$ \textbf{escrever}
  \item \emph{schola} $\to$ \textbf{escola} (\textquotedblleft{}school\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{stāre} $\to$ \textbf{estar} — the being-verb you already have
  \item \emph{spērāre} $\to$ \textbf{esperar} (\textquotedblleft{}to wait, to hope\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{spatium} $\to$ \textbf{espaço}
\end{itemize}

So when a Portuguese word opens with \textbf{es-} and the rest of it resembles an English word missing its \emph{e}, it usually is one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}escrevo, escreves, escreve, escrevemos, escrevem\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Já escrevi a carta\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Está escrito\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter's four, first person — \textquotedblleft{}penso, entendo, leio, escrevo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the propped-up e — \textquotedblleft{}escrever · escola · estar · esperar\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{escrever}. (\textbf{Escrevo, escreves, escreve, escrevemos, escrevem}.) What is its past participle? (\emph{\textbf{Escrito}} — Latin \emph{scriptum}.) What did \emph{scrībere} mean literally? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{scratch}\textquotedblright{}.) Why \emph{escola} and not \emph{scola}? (Iberian Romance \textbf{propped an e-} in front of \emph{sc-}, \emph{sp-}, \emph{st-}.) Which verb of being got the same treatment? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}, from \emph{stāre}.) Now the four verbs of this chapter, in the \emph{eu} form. (\textbf{Penso, entendo, leio, escrevo}.) Next: taking.
\end{tcolorbox}
